Designed to complement classroom learning, this experience offers students the opportunity to apply theoretical knowledge in real-world veterinary settings. Under the guidance of experienced veterinary professionals, participants will gain practical skills in animal care, medical procedures, and client interaction. subject: Apprentice: Mechanical Insulation
description: PROGRAM: Apprenticeship Technology - Building Trades   LECTURE HOURS MIN: 3  DATE OF LAST REVISION: Fall 2022   This course is designed to enhance the working knowledge of traditional methods of craftsmanship and contemporary methods and materials for masonry preservation repairs.   The core modules include Fundamentals of Historic Preservation, Mortars in Preservation,  Introduction to Architecture & Building Technology and Historic Structure Survey & Condition Repair.  The program is designed to elevate the level of workmanship of the students and allow them to maintain a competitive edge in the  growing restoration field. subject: American Sign Language (AMSL)
description: PROGRAM: Foreign Languages   LECTURE HOURS MIN: 4  DATE OF LAST REVISION: Fall, 2018   American Sign Language I is an introduction to ASL as it is used within the deaf culture. Students will learn the basic grammatical structure of the language and basic communication skills including finger spelling, facial expressions and non-manual behaviors. Students will gain an understanding of the history and development of deaf culture, its values and literature. Students will be able to demonstrate the ability to communicate sign language at a basic, introductory level. Class activities will include the use of storytelling as a way for students to practice and read ASL.   MAJOR COURSE LEARNING OBJECTIVES: Upon successful completion of this course the student will be expected to:  Demonstrate one’s understanding of the early historical development of deaf communities through recognition of deaf and hearing leaders.Identify the historical significance of Gallaudet University and its political influence.Contrast deaf culture/community values with hearing culture values.Demonstrate one’s understanding for the deaf perspective on living in a hearing world.Demonstrate one’s understanding of the role of sign language in deaf humor and literature.Examine basic linguistic features of ASL as a language different from English.Produce and demonstrate the ability to communicate sign language at a basic, introductory level.Construct and compose the basic grammar structure of sentences in ASL to include the use of facial expression and non-manual behaviors.Accurately formulate and express the vocabulary of ASL beyond five word phrases.Relate the origins of the sign.Distinguish the difference between the different forms of sign language.Utilize transition verbs in the appropriate context.   COURSE CONTENT: Topical areas of study include -  Culture related topicsASL characteristicsFacial expression and non-manual behaviorsFinger-spellingGrammatical structure and syntaxSkill developmentVocabulary, time periods, and tenses Course Addendum - Syllabus (Click to expand)

subject: American Sign Language (AMSL)
description: PREREQUISITES: AMSL 101 - American Sign Language I   PROGRAM: World Languages   LECTURE HOURS MIN: 4  DATE OF LAST REVISION: Fall, 2018   American Sign Language II is designed to provide a continuation of the introductory course. Students will increase their knowledge of the deaf community, culture, and deaf education in a hearing world. The deaf perspective on traditional employment of deaf people in a hearing society will be explored. In language development, complex grammar functions, expanded vocabulary, and skill development are incorporated into the use of sign production. Students will be exposed to the controversial cochlear implant and how it is affecting the deaf and their culture. description: PREREQUISITES: Demonstrated competency through appropriate assessment or earning a grade of “C” or better in ENGL 093 - Introduction to College Writing  and ENGL 083 - Reading Strategies for College  or ENGL 095 - Integrated Reading and Writing   PROGRAM: Social Sciences   LECTURE HOURS MIN: 3  DATE OF LAST REVISION: Fall 2021   Human Origins is the scientific study of human biological and cultural evolution from early pre-Pleistocene hominids through the development of urbanized state societies. MAJOR COURSE LEARNING OBJECTIVES: Upon successful completion of this course the student will be expected to:  Describe the major fields of anthropology, with emphasis on physical anthropology.Describe the history of evolutionary thought and demonstrate a critical appraisal of natural selection as the principal mechanism for evolution.Describe the structure and function of DNA, genes, and how information in DNA is translated into proteins.Demonstrate knowledge of the basic principles of Mendelian inheritance and how they relate to humans.Demonstrate knowledge of how primates are classified.Describe the characteristics of the Order Primates and the major features of prosimians and anthropoids.Describe primate social behavior with respect to dominance, communication, sexual behavior, play and hunting.Describe how fossils are dated.Identify characteristics associated with the following groups of hominids: Australopithecines, early Homo, Homo erectus, Neanderthals, Homo Floresiensis, Denisovans, Homo Naledi, and Homo sapiens.Arrange the various groups of hominids in a chronological timeline from the earliest specimens to the most recent.Summarize the current theories regarding the origin and dispersal of modern humans.Describe the origin of agriculture and the domestication of plants and animals.Describe the development of urbanized state societies.Demonstrate knowledge of the adaptive significance of human variation.Demonstrate knowledge of the biological meaning of race and objections to the use of the word in anthropology. PROGRAM: Diagnostic Medical Sonography   LAB HOURS MIN: 6  TOTAL CONTACT HOURS MIN: 6  DATE OF LAST REVISION: Fall 2022   This lab will introduce the students to basic concepts of sonography, machine controls and exam protocols. Image optimization and patient care skill will be applied during this time. Content and lab practice shall be assigned for sequential development, application, critical analysis, and evaluation of concepts and theories in the performance of general sonographic procedures. The structured lab practice will prepare the student to for the clinical experience, competency-based assignments in the clinical setting, concepts of teamwork and patient care.  Lab performance and skills will be evaluated in a similar fashion as evaluation in the clinical setting. Patient care and scanning skills as well as proper ergonomic techniques are learned and practiced in the lab.   MAJOR COURSE LEARNING OBJECTIVES: Demonstrate principles of professional ethics.  Demonstrate professional communication with instructors and peers. React to criticism constructively and demonstrate the desire to improve. Demonstrate practice and basic understanding of common exams. Perform basic routine scans to show clinical readiness. Perform sonographic examinations using proper ergonomic techniques. Demonstrate knowledge of knobology and image optimization techniques. Understand routine patient care skills and regulations such as HIPAA and ALARA.COURSE CONTENT: Topical areas of study include - Organs and systems covered in DMSI 135 as well as other structures and systems not covered. The student is to practice and gain competence in assigned structures, but also gain knowledge and experience in any other exams involved in during the lab experience. Scanning techniques will cover: Ultrasound terminology Ultrasound knobology Basic echocardiographic windows and views

subject: Diagnostic Med Sonog (DMSI)
course_name: Cardiac Sonography III and Clinical Orientation Lab III
description: PREREQUISITES: DMSI 136  PROGRAM: Diagnostic Medical Sonography   LECTURE HOURS MIN: 1  LAB HOURS MIN: 1  TOTAL CONTACT HOURS MIN: 2  DATE OF LAST REVISION: Fall 2022   This course will continue to build on the principles learned in Cardiac Sonography I and II with a review of cardiac anatomy and cross-sectional anatomy. Valvular heart disease and cardiomyopathies will be discussed. Testing methods and correlations will be explained. Alternate cardiac imaging methods will be discussed.   MAJOR COURSE LEARNING OBJECTIVES: 1.  Describe and demonstrate normal valvular evaluation.  2.  Describe pathophysiologic effects of valvular disease and the methods of evaluation for regurgitation and stenosis. 3.  Describe and demonstrate the evaluation methods and pathophysiologic effects of cardiomyopathy diseases on the heart. 4.  Demonstrate and define advanced methods of left and right heart assessment when disease is present. 5.  Understand and demonstrate the normal great vessel evaluation, recognize pathophysiologic effects, and demonstrate methods of pathology evaluation. 6.  Understand the rationale and methods for obtaining measurements to quantify the flow in the normal and abnormal heart. 7.  Demonstrate the methods and rationale for using the ped-off probe in the presence of pathology. 8.  Identify, describe and correlate alternate testing methods such as MRI, CT, angiography, nuclear medicine and radiography studies. 9.  Demonstrate an understanding of differential diagnoses of pathologies covered in this course.COURSE CONTENT: Topical areas of study include - Sonographic quantitative and qualitative methods of cardiac evaluation Sonographic evaluation of cardiomyopathies Sonographic evaluation of diseases of the cardiac valves Study of pathophysiologic effects of disease on the heart Alternate imaging modalities

subject: Diagnostic Med Sonog (DMSI)
course_name: Cardiac Sonography IV and Clinical Orientation Lab IV
description: PREREQUISITES: DMSI 139  PROGRAM: Diagnostic Medical Sonography   LECTURE HOURS MIN: 1  LAB HOURS MIN: 2  TOTAL CONTACT HOURS MIN: 3  DATE OF LAST REVISION: Fall 2022   This course will continue to build on the principles learned in Cardiac Sonography I, II and III with a review of cardiac anatomy.  Pericardial disease, pulmonary hypertension, endocardial disease, aortic and great vessel disease, coronary artery or ischemic disease will be covered and discussed.   MAJOR COURSE LEARNING OBJECTIVES: 1.  Describe and understand the methods of evaluation of pericardial disease, endocardial pathologies and the pathophysiologic effects of the diseases.  2.  Describe the appearance and pathophysiologic effects of pulmonary hypertension and coronary artery disease as well as the methods of evaluation. 3.  Understand and demonstrate the normal great vessel evaluation as well as recognize pathophysiologic effects and demonstrate methods of pathology evaluation. 4.  Understand the rationale and methods for obtaining measurements to quantify the flow in the normal and abnormal heart. 5.  Demonstrate an understanding of differential diagnoses of pathologies covered in this course.COURSE CONTENT: Topical areas of study include - Sonographic quantitative and qualitative methods of cardiac evaluation Sonographic evaluation of pericardial and endocardial diseases Sonographic evaluation cardiac ischemic disease and pulmonary hypertension Sonographic evaluation of diseases of pulmonary vasculature and great vessels Study of pathophysiologic effects of disease on the heart

subject: Diagnostic Med Sonog (DMSI)
description: PREREQUISITES: DMSI 136 or DMSI 151  PROGRAM: Diagnostic Medical Sonography   LECTURE HOURS MIN: 1  LAB HOURS MIN: 1.5  TOTAL CONTACT HOURS MIN: 2.5  DATE OF LAST REVISION: Fall 2022   This course introduces the student to the principles of hemodynamics in the heart and throughout the cardiovascular system. The physical principles of blood flow and the pathophysiologic effects are discussed. Waveform analysis and mathematical computation of formulas related to blood flow are explained.   MAJOR COURSE LEARNING OBJECTIVES: 1.  Understand basic physics principles of blood flow.  2.  Describe the flow of blood throughout the cardiovascular system. 3.  Demonstrate an understanding of the effects of loading conditions on the heart as well as the pathophysiologic effects of loading and intracardiac pressures. 4.  Identify the pathophysiologic effects on blood flow. 5.  Demonstrate the methods for obtaining proper blood flow measurements. 6.  Demonstrate the understanding of improper Doppler gate effects on blood flow measurements. 7.  Describe pathologic Doppler waveforms from the cardiovascular system. 8.  Use hemodynamic formulas to calculate flow in normal and pathologic conditions.COURSE CONTENT: Topical areas of study include - Hemodynamic principles Cardiovascular blood flow Cardiovascular effects on blood flow Normal and abnormal Doppler waveforms

course_name: Cardiac Sonography V and Clinical Orientation Lab V
description: PREREQUISITES: DMSI 140  PROGRAM: Diagnostic Medical Sonography   LECTURE HOURS MIN: 1  LAB HOURS MIN: 1.5  TOTAL CONTACT HOURS MIN: 2.5  DATE OF LAST REVISION: Fall 2022   Areas to be covered in this course are prosthetic valves, cardiac anatomy with relation to tumors, congenital anomalies, contrast enhancement with guidelines, interventional cardiac procedures and intracardiac devices, and cardiac catheterization. Cardiac medications and uses will be discussed.   MAJOR COURSE LEARNING OBJECTIVES: 1.  Describe cardiac contrast uses, methods, rationale, standards, limitations, guidelines, and regulations.  2.  Demonstrate the processes performed with the use of cardiac contrast. 3.  Identify different cardiac pharmacologic medication uses, limitations, effects, contraindications, and methods of administration. 4.  Identify different prosthetic valves, appearances, normal function and pathophysiologic effects of the diseased prosthetic valves. 5.  Define different methods of prosthetic valve evaluation. 6.  Describe and define cardiac masses, tumors, and the pathophysiologic effects of these disease processes. 7.  Describe and identify congenital anomalies with various post-surgical appearances and the pathophysiologic effect of pre-surgical and post-surgical corrections. 8.  Describe and identify intracardiac devices, shunts, cardiac assist devices, and procedures used related to the devices. 9.  Identify the processes, needs, rationale, imagery and procedures used in cardiac catheterization procedures. 10.  Understand differential diagnoses of pathologies covered in this course.COURSE CONTENT: Topical areas of study include - Pathologies associated with heart transplants, cancerous conditions, and systemic diseases Methods used in the cardiac patient catheterization Prosthetic valves Methods used with cardiac contrast Adult congenital heart Interventional and intracardiac procedures

description: PREREQUISITES: DMSI 144  PROGRAM: Diagnostic Medical Sonography   LECTURE HOURS MIN: 1  LAB HOURS MIN: 1.5  TOTAL CONTACT HOURS MIN: 2.5  DATE OF LAST REVISION: Fall 2022   Covered in this course are topics to include: transesophageal echocardiography, cardio-oncology, systemic diseases, transplant and associated conditions, stress echocardiography, and cardiac trauma. Three-dimensional cardiac ultrasound and strain measurements associated with conditions will be covered.   MAJOR COURSE LEARNING OBJECTIVES: 1.  Describe the uses, processes, and physics behind 3-D echocardiography.  2.  Describe and demonstrate the methods and processes of both exercise and pharmacologic stress echocardiography. 3.  Identify multiple systemic disease processes, pathophysiologic effects as well as monitoring of such conditions. 4.  Describe the process and identify the images of transesophageal echocardiography. 5.  Demonstrate the sonographer’s role, methods and processes used in transesophageal echocardiography. 6.  Identify considerations of the transplanted heart, associated conditions, and post-surgical appearances. 7.  Identify post-surgical pathophysiologic effects on the transplanted heart. 8.  Describe the role of echocardiography in cardio-oncology. 9.  Describe methods and exam processes used with cardiac trauma patients. 10.  Understand differential diagnoses of pathologies covered in this course. 11.  Define and understand cardiac strain and speckle tracking methods, uses, and efficacy in certain patients.COURSE CONTENT: Topical areas of study include - Pathologies with transplanted heart, cancerous conditions, and systemic diseases Methods used in the cardiac patient such as transesophageal echocardiography, 3D, and strain Cardiac trauma Stress echocardiography Transesophageal echocardiography

subject: Diagnostic Med Sonog (DMSI)
course_name: Vascular Sonography I and Clinical Orientation Lab I
description: PREREQUISITES: Admission to the DMSI program.  PROGRAM: Diagnostic Medical Sonography   LECTURE HOURS MIN: 1  LAB HOURS MIN: 2  TOTAL CONTACT HOURS MIN: 3  DATE OF LAST REVISION: Fall 2022   This course will focus on the cerebrovascular system to include anatomy, physiology, and pathology. Normal and pathological conditions will be discussed as well as the pathophysiologic effects of the disease on the cerebrovascular system. Introduction to the Doppler wave forms normally seen in the cerebrovascular system will be discussed. Terminology used in the vascular testing process will be discussed.   MAJOR COURSE LEARNING OBJECTIVES: 1.  Understand the role of noninvasive vascular testing in the diagnosis of vascular disease in the cerebrovascular system.  2.  Describe the sonographic appearance of the normal and abnormal cerebrovascular system. 3.  Define the normal waveforms in the cerebrovascular system. 4.  Relate findings to the underlying anatomy/physiology and other changes attributable to vascular disease. 5.  Explain the pathophysiologic effect of vascular disease on the cerebrovascular system. 6.  Understand the important elements of composing and generating preliminary and final reports using correct terminology. 7.  Describe the required protocol for imaging the cerebrovascular system using ultrasound.COURSE CONTENT: Topical areas of study include - Cerebrovascular anatomy and pathology Cerebrovascular hemodynamics Scanning protocols and techniques of the cerebrovascular system

There will be a study of the upper and lower peripheral arterial system to include the anatomy, physiology, pathology, hemodynamics, and pathophysiology. Pathologies of the organ structures are covered as well as pathophysiologic effects on organs, systems, hemodynamics and sonographic and Doppler appearances. COURSE CONTENT: Topical areas of study include - Topical areas of study include -  Upper and lower arterial systemsHemodynamics and Doppler techniques for peripheral arterial systemsScanning protocols and techniques of the peripheral arterial systemExercise testingPenile Doppler and testingAtherosclerosis and diseases effecting the peripheral arterial systemsExtrinsic pathology affecting the peripheral arterial systemsBypass graft evaluations Arterial anatomy of the upper and lower extremityDisease processes of the arterial systemDoppler and plethysmography testing procedures for the upper and lower extremities Course Addendum - Syllabus (Click to expand)

subject: Diagnostic Med Sonog (DMSI)
course_name: Vascular Sonography II and Clinical Orientation Lab II
description: PREREQUISITES: DMSI 149  PROGRAM: Diagnostic Medical Sonography   LECTURE HOURS MIN: 1  LAB HOURS MIN: 1  TOTAL CONTACT HOURS MIN: 2  DATE OF LAST REVISION: Fall 2022   This course is a continuation of the studies of the cerebrovascular system and will focus on the principles of hemodynamics and how disease affects these principles. Waveform analysis in the normal and abnormal system will be defined. Transcranial Doppler methods and uses will be covered. Interpretation of the waveforms and exam findings will be explained. Standards affecting the vascular sonographer and the cerebrovascular system will be discussed. Alternate imaging modalities will be covered. Terminology applied to sonography of the cerebrovascular system will be explained.   MAJOR COURSE LEARNING OBJECTIVES: 1.  Describe the rules of hemodynamics and how pathology changes these rules.  2.  Understand the role of noninvasive vascular testing in the diagnosis of vascular disease in the cerebrovascular system. 3.  Differentiate between normal and abnormal B-mode and Doppler findings. 4.  Relate findings to the underlying anatomy/physiology and other changes attributable to vascular disease. 5.  Use recommended interpretation criteria, understanding their value and limitations. 6.  Understand the important elements of composing and generating preliminary and final reports using correct terminology. 7.  Understand various regulatory issues affecting the vascular ultrasound profession. 8.  Describe treatment methods used in cerebrovascular disease. 9.  Describe the processes of alternate imaging processes and their role in the patient’s care as well as limitations of these exams. 10.  Use terminology applicable to the sonographer and the vascular system.COURSE CONTENT: Topical areas of study include - Cerebrovascular hemodynamics Pathologic effects on cerebrovascular hemodynamics Scanning protocols and techniques of the cerebrovascular system Interpretation guidelines Alternate imaging modalities Applicable terminology

course_name: Vascular Sonography V and Clinical Orientation Lab V
description: PREREQUISITES: DMSI 156  PROGRAM: Diagnostic Medical Sonography   LECTURE HOURS MIN: 1  LAB HOURS MIN: 1.5  TOTAL CONTACT HOURS MIN: 2.5  DATE OF LAST REVISION: Fall 2022   Studies will include the upper and lower peripheral venous systems and the abdominal vascular system. These studies will include anatomy, physiology, and pathophysiology of these systems. Hemodialysis graft analysis will also be defined and explained. Venous insufficiency causes, testing, and treatment options will be discussed. Alternate imaging methods and testing will be discussed. Medication usage and effects in the therapeutic patient state will be explained.   MAJOR COURSE LEARNING OBJECTIVES: 1.  Describe anatomy of the venous systems of the upper and lower extremities.  2.  Describe pathology and physiology of the venous system of the extremities. 3.  Describe normal and pathological waveforms in the venous system. 4.  Explain the venous scanning protocol. 5.  Differentiate and explain the different methods used in the diagnosis of venous insufficiency. 6.  Understand the treatment options for venous disease. 7.  Describe the anatomy and function of hemodialysis grafts. 8.  Summarize and explain the process of hemodialysis graft analysis. 9.  Describe normal waveforms of hemodialysis grafts. 10.  Define the hemodynamic effects of graft immaturity or failure. 11.  Define vascular imaging alternative processes and the limitations of the exams. 12.  Describe medications used most commonly in patients with vascular diseases.COURSE CONTENT: Topical areas of study include - Study of upper and lower extremity venous anatomy, physiology, and pathology Scanning protocols for upper and lower venous systems Hemodialysis graft analysis

subject: Diagnostic Med Sonog (DMSI)
description: PREREQUISITES: DMSI 107 - Cardiac Sonography I and Lab   PROGRAM: Diagnostic Medical Sonography   LECTURE HOURS MIN: 3  LAB HOURS MIN: 2  DATE OF LAST REVISION: Spring, 2021   This course will continue to build on the principles learned in Cardiac Sonography I with a review of cardiac anatomy and cross sectional anatomy. description: PREREQUISITES: BUSN 160 - Introduction to Insurance   PROGRAM: Business Administration   LECTURE HOURS MIN: 3  DATE OF LAST REVISION: Fall, 2014   Analyzes personal loss exposures and insurance including homeowners and other dwelling coverages, personal liability, inland marine, auto, life, health insurance, and financial planning.   MAJOR COURSE LEARNING OBJECTIVES: Upon successful completion of this course the student will be expected to:  Describe and analyze the property loss exposures that individuals and families might face in regard to the property exposed to loss and the causes of loss affecting property, and the financial consequences of property losses.Describe and analyze the liability loss exposures that individuals and families might face in regard to the possibility of a claim for money damages and the financial consequences of liability losses.Describe and analyze the risk management process that can be used by individuals and families in regard to the steps in the risk management process, insurance as a risk management technique, and other techniques to treat loss exposures.Describe the various problems associated with automobile insurance which include the high frequency of automobile accidents, the high costs of automobile accidents. The substantial underwriting losses incurred by insurers, irresponsible drivers, and the availability and affordability of automobile insurance.Describe, analyze and explain the major functions of the personal auto policy which include personal automobile insurance and personal loss exposures, liability coverage, medical payment coverage, and the uninsured motorist’s coverage.Describe, analyze and explain the major functions of the personal auto policy which include physical damage insurance for the damage or theft of a covered auto, the duties imposed on an insured after an accident or loss, bankruptcy of the insured, changes in the policy, fraud, legal action against the insurer, and the various endorsements that can be added to the personal auto policy.Describe and explain the homeowner’s policy series which includes the homeowner’s declarations, insuring agreement, definitions, and Section I of the HO-3 policy.Describe and explain the homeowner’s policy series which includes Section II of the HO-3 policy, including personal liability and medical payments to others.Demonstrate and discuss the different homeowner’s forms, the need for homeowner’s endorsements, the endorsements used to modify homeowner’s coverages, and the various factors used in rating homeowner’s policies.Demonstrate knowledge of miscellaneous residential loss exposures, the differences between the HO-3 and DP-3 policies, the Insurance Service Office (ISO) homeowners endorsements used for mobile homes and farms, etc.Demonstrate and discuss the characteristics, provisions and exclusions, and coverage of inland marine floaters.Describe and discuss the different types of personal loss exposures, the process of financial planning and investing to attain financial goals, process of financial planning and investing to attain financial goals, retirement planning and tax deferred retirement plans, and the basic characteristics and benefits of the Social Security system.Describe and distinguish between the various types of individual and group medical, dental, and disability insurance policies as well as health care providers and government health insurance programs. description: PREREQUISITES: Demonstrated competency through appropriate assessment or earning a grade of “C” or better in ENGL 093 - Introduction to College Writing  and ENGL 083 - Reading Strategies for College  or ENGL 095 - Integrated Reading and Writing   PROGRAM: Service Learning   LECTURE HOURS MIN: 1  LAB HOURS MIN: 2  DATE OF LAST REVISION: Summer, 2012   EPICS is a service-learning design course in which teams of students from across campus work together on long-term projects that benefit the community. Project work centers on the engineering/technology/computing needs of a community partner, but interdisciplinary team interaction is an integral element for project success. Students may participate in EPICS multiple semesters and participation for multiple consecutive semesters on a project team is encouraged. Teams are composed of first year and second year students. COURSE CONTENT: Topical areas of study include -  Multidisciplinary Design: Learn how to be better designers, gain design knowledge and skills;Learn how to apply disciplinary knowledge to real and possibly ill-defined problems;Learn how to identify and acquire new knowledge;Learn to collaborate with people from other disciplines and develop an appreciation for cross-disciplinary contributions in design. subject: Advanced Manufacturing (ADMF)
description: PROGRAM: Advanced Automation and Robotics Technology   LECTURE HOURS MIN: 2  LAB HOURS MIN: 2  DATE OF LAST REVISION: Fall 2022   Introduces the basic principles and practices of Safety and Quality used in manufacturing environments. description: PREREQUISITES/COREQUISITE: INDT 203 Machine Maintenance and Installation   PROGRAM: Advanced Automation and Robotics Technology   LECTURE HOURS MIN: 2  LAB HOURS MIN: 2  DATE OF LAST REVISION: Fall 2022   This course covers the basics of mechanical components and electrical drives in a complex mechatronic system. Based upon a physical system, students will learn the basic functions and physical properties of mechanical components as well as electrical drives (AC and DC), and the roles they play within the system. They will also learn about mechanical components which lead and support the energy through a mechanical system to increase efficiency and to reduce wear and tear. Materials, lubrication requirements and surface properties will be examined. Technical documentation such as data sheets and specifications of mechanical elements and electrical drives will also be covered. By understanding the inner workings of the complete system, students will learn and apply troubleshooting strategies to identify, localize and (where possible) to correct malfunctions. Preventive maintenance of mechanical elements and electrical drives as well as safety issues within the system will be discussed. This course will use lecture, lab, and online simulation to prepare students for certification assessment through SACA, Smart Automation Certification Alliance.   MAJOR COURSE LEARNING OBJECTIVES: Upon successful completion of this course the student will be expected to:  Understand the hazards of electromechanical equipment and apply safe working practices. [f]Describe the basic physical properties of mechanical components including; materials, lubrication requirements, and surface properties. [f]Carry out adjustments on mechanical components in a mechatronic system. [e]Read, analyze and utilize the the technical data sheets for the mechanical components and electrical drives within a mechatronic system. [f]Correctly localize, identify and document causes of malfunctions in mechanical components or electrical drives, based upon the technical documentation. [b,e]Correct malfunctions where possible, or correctly identify the expertise required to correct a malfunction. [b,e]Transfer the knowledge learned from one system to another system. [b,e]Effectively use current and emerging computer technologies when applicable. [a]Demonstrate ability to read and interpret technical documents. [b,e]Demonstrate ability to use various types of software applicable to course. description: PREREQUISITES: ECED 103, Curriculum in Early Childhood Classroom and ENGL 111, English Composition  PROGRAM: Early Childhood Education   LECTURE HOURS MIN: 3  LAB HOURS MIN: 1  DATE OF LAST REVISION: Fall 2023   Explores the aspects of early literacy based on the Science of Reading and language skill development in young children from birth through third grade to foster a love for reading and promote the enjoyment of literature by cultivating engaging and diverse reading experiences that captivate individuals, enhance their imagination, and instill a lifelong appreciation for the written word.  The course identifies developmentally appropriate  practices and materials provided in the learning environment that support meaningful speech, listening skills and fundamental concept development about print as related to research based reading instruction across the early childhood age range of birth to age 8 Students are required to complete observations and field experiences with children as related to this course (32 hours; 16 lab hours/16 hours of field experience with school age, K-3).  Students are required to meet volunteer standards for public school settings, which may vary according to their field placement.MAJOR COURSE LEARNING OBJECTIVES: Upon successful completion of this course the student will be expected to: Review the importance of research for educators and the role research has in informing teaching. 1.1 Review the importance of research for educators. 1.2 Discuss the role research has in informing teaching and influencing reading outcomes historically to present date including the differences between Science of Reading and Whole Language. (KPS 1.6) 1.3 Discuss research in support of play based learning for early oral language development for young children.  Review Indiana laws related to K-3 reading instruction. 2.1 Locate and examine Indiana laws related to reading instruction. 2.2 Locate and examine IN DOE rules regarding teacher training and certification in Science of Reading. 2.3 Discuss reading outcomes for students in Indiana and in the US.  Describe the foundational concepts of literacy acquisition, including the language processing requirements, the importance of explicit reading instruction, and the factors influencing literacy development. (1a, 4b, 4c) 3.1 Discuss the use of the Simple View of Reading in guiding assessment and instruction. 3.2  Review the five essential literacy skills and describe the reciprocal relationships among phonemic awareness, decoding, word recognition, spelling, and vocabulary knowledge. (KPS 1.3). 3.3 Explore Scarborough’s Reading Rope. 3.4 Describe the language processing requirements of proficient reading and writing: phonological, orthographic, semantic, syntactic, and discourse (four part processing model). (KPS 1.1) 3.5 Explain aspects of cognition and behavior that affect reading and writing development. (KPS 1.4) 3.6 Explain phases and progression of skills in the typical developmental progression of oral language, phoneme awareness, decoding skills, printed word recognition, spelling, reading fluency, reading comprehension, and written expression. (KPS 1.8, 1.9)  Identify and define the emergence of speech and auditory skills in children, birth through third grade and the role of receptive and expressive language in oral and written language comprehension. (1a, 1b, 1c) 4.1 Identify the emergence of speech and auditory skills in young children. 4.2  Define the differences and roles of receptive and expressive language.4.3 Explain the importance and role of vocabulary development in the early years.4.4 Discuss opportunities to use sign language with infants/toddlers as a means of early expressive communication.4.5 Model ways to build oral language development with birth-Prek aged children.4.6 Discuss ways in which families can support the emergence of language development with their young child.4.7 Explain the contribution of environmental factors to literacy outcomes (e.g., language spoken at home, language and literacy experiences, cultural values).4.8 Identify resources for supporting literacy acquisition among students with language variations.4.9  Discuss warning signs for early language development delays and recognize when there is a need for early intervention.  Identify print awareness strategies for children ages 3-8. (1a, 1d, 3a, 3b) 5.1 Observe children to determine their level of print awareness. 5.2 Engage children in activities to support print awareness.5.3 Complete a print awareness assessment with a child, meet with the family to set a goal, and create an instructional activity based on the child’s individual needs. (NAEYC Key Assessment)5.4 Examine and discuss literacy rich environments and the importance for young children. Recognize the diverse reading profiles, including dyslexia, and how they vary in presentation, degree, and response to development and instruction. (1c, 1d, 4b)6.1 Review warning signs including delayed oral language skills and family history for early language development delays including common intrinsic differences for good and poor readers. (KPS 1.7) 6.2 Identify the distinguishing characteristics of dyslexia. (KPS 2.3) 6.3 Describe how reading disabilities vary in presentation and degree. (KPS 2.4) 6.4  Explain how and why symptoms of reading difficulty are likely to change over time in response to development and instruction. (KPS 2.5)  Analyze and apply various types of assessments, including screening, progress-monitoring, diagnostic, and outcome assessments, to identify and support students at risk for reading difficulties. (3a, 3b, 3c, 3d, 6c, 6d) 7.1 Review the differences among and purposes for screening, progress-monitoring, diagnostic, and outcome assessments. (KPS 3.1) 7.2 Explore informal diagnostic surveys of oral reading fluency, comprehension, spelling, and writing. (KPS 3.6) 7.3 Discuss how assessment data is shared with students, parents, and other teachers. (KPS 3.8)  Explore systems of support, including Multi-tiered Systems of Support (MTSS), First Steps, family engagement, etc.  in the prevention and remediation of academic and behavior difficulties. (2b, 3d, 6b, 6c) 8.1 Develop culturally responsive emerging literacy activities for the home that support families in understanding the benefits of reading aloud to children, and support parent/child engagement with books and oral language for children ages birth-grade 3.  (2a, 2b, 4a) 8.2 Discuss the process for working with families and other professionals to determine potential delays, screenings, and next steps. (KPS 3.8) 8.3 Discuss the impacts of early hearing or vision loss, and the importance of hearing, vision, and literacy screening. 8.4 Discuss the importance of interventions for struggling readers at the end of 1st grade. 8.5 Examine how reading difficulties can be prevented with intentional experiences in PreK. 8.6 Recognize and discuss how quality reading instruction is trauma informed care. description: PREREQUISITES: ECED 103 - Curriculum in the Early Childhood Classroom  , ECED 120 - Child Growth and Development   PROGRAM: Early Childhood Education   LECTURE HOURS MIN: 3  LAB HOURS MIN: 1  DATE OF LAST REVISION: Fall 2023   Review cognitive theories of development in relation to the domains of early learning.  Analyze appropriate problem solving, math, science, and social studies curriculum in early childhood settings.  Create and implement curriculum in the domains of early learning utilizing appropriate child outcomes assessment.  Reflect upon implementation of activities and assessment with children.  Students are required to complete observations and field experiences with children (32 hours) as related to this course and be evaluated by the course instructor.  Students are required to meet personnel requirements for child care licensing which may include, but are not limited to:  FBI fingerprints, 5 panel drug screen, TB test, physical/vaccination history, criminal history checks, CPS registry checks, reference checks, health and safety protocols, and completion of the ILEAD mandatory training modules- Health and Safety Modules 1-4, Intro to the Indiana Early Learning Standards, and Child Abuse Prevention and Detection.MAJOR COURSE LEARNING OBJECTIVES: Upon successful completion of this course the student will be expected to: Review and identify theories, principles and research that serve as a guide toimplementation of best practices in support of cognitive development in young children. (1a, 3a, 4b ) 1.1 Describe theoretical perspectives and core research of the developmental periods of early childhood and how development and learning intersect across domains. (1a leveling)1.2 Review how structural inequities and trauma adversely impact development and learning. (1c leveling)1.3 Review the core research base regarding the purposes and uses of assessment. (3a leveling, KPS 3.1 )1.4 Summarize the foundational theories of cognitive development (e.g., Piaget’s stages of cognitive development, Vygotsky’s sociocultural theory, information processing theory). Describe brain development in young children including executive function, learning motivation, and approaches to play and learning. (1a, 4b) 2.1 Define executive function and list ways to support it. (4b leveling, KPS 2.4)2.2 Define learning motivation and list ways to promote it.2.3 Define approaches to play and learning.2.4 Describe brain development for children ages 0-3. (1a leveling) 2.5 Describe brain development for children ages 3-5. (1a leveling) 2.6 Describe brain development and the brain science behind learning to read. (KPS 1.2) Observe a selected age group of children and plan developmentally appropriate learning activities/lessons.(3a, 3b, 3c) 3.1 Identify that observation and documentation are central practices in assessment.3.2 Practice ethical observation skills to observe a group of children to determine needs and interests.3.3 Describe how young children learn across core content areas and use this understanding to make instructional decisions (5b leveling)3.4 Use observations to write goals and objectives in alignment with Indiana Early Learning Standards. 3.5 Plan developmentally appropriate, hands-on activities for a group of children based on needs and interests gathered through observation in the areas of math, science, and social studies that counters biases and stereotypes and fosters children’s interest in the content area. (5c leveling) 3.6 Implement teaching practices that incorporate various types of play and support children’s executive functioning skills. (4b leveling) 3.7 Plan integrated curriculum that incorporates math, science, and/or social studies with Science of Reading literacy based strategies for language and vocabulary development (KPS 4E.3, 4E.4). Observe and analyze environments and activities in relation to children’s learning.  (1b, 3c, 3d) 4.1 Observe and analyze classroom environments for children ages 0-3 to determine what materials, activities, and interactions are provided to support cognitive development.4.2 Observe and analyze classroom environments for children ages 3-5 to determine what materials, activities, and interactions are provided to support cognitive development.4.3 Observe and analyze classroom environments for children in grades K-3 to determine what materials, activities, and interactions are provided to support cognitive development. 4.4 Explore the role of the educator in creating a stimulating environment that encourages exploration, curiosity, critical thinking, and language development . Plan, implement and evaluate integrated learning experiences for young children which promote math, science and social studies skills and further support language and literacy development. (1d, 4a, 4b, 4c, 5a, KPS 4a, 4e) 5.1 Combine understanding of content knowledge and pedagogical knowledge to select and create activities to support the integration of content areas. (5c leveling)5.2 Use teaching practices that are developmentally appropriate including level of development, individual characteristics, and the sociocultural context in which they live (4b leveling) 5.3  Integrate activities to support vocabulary development and age appropriate strategies for listening or reading comprehension with math, science, and social studies concepts and activities (KPS 4F.3, 4F.4, 4F.5) 5.3 Critique a learning experience after implementation for how it supported math, science and social studies skills and language and literacy development.  Plan, implement, and evaluate learning experiences that support deep vocabulary development within integrated experiences for math, science, and social studies. (1d, 4a, 4b, 4c, 5a)6.1 Identify essential vocabulary terms specific to math, science, and social studies topics being taught and prioritize vocabulary that is fundamental to understanding core concepts in each subject area (KPS 4E.3, 4E.4). 6.2 Design lesson plans that seamlessly integrate vocabulary instruction with math, science, and social studies content and incorporate vocabulary into hands-on activities, experiments, and project-based learning (KPS 4E.3, 4E.4).6.3 Explicitly teach new vocabulary using developmentally appropriate strategies that encourage active participation (KPS 4E.3, 4E.4). 6.4 Critique your learning experience after implementing how deep vocabulary was integrated.  Prepare multi-sensory and multi-modal learning experiences for children.7.1 Recognize the different sensory modalities (visual, auditory, kinesthetic, tactile) that children may prefer in their learning experiences (4A.2).7.2 Integrate tools and manipulatives that engage multiple senses simultaneously (e.g., sandpaper letters for tactile-kinesthetic learning) (4A.2).7.3 Deliver lessons that incorporate a blend of auditory, visual, and kinesthetic learning opportunities to accommodate diverse learners and use storytelling, role-playing, and interactive demonstrations to engage children in multi-modal experiences (4A.2). 7.4 Ensure that multi-sensory and multi-modal learning experiences are accessible to all children, including those with sensory processing disorders or other special needs, and adapt and differentiate activities to ensure inclusivity and support for diverse learners (4A.2).  Explore the use of technology in the classroom as a teacher resource, and learning opportunity for children. (6c) 8.1 Describe the structure, strengths, and limitations of a variety of assessment methods and tools including technology related tools. (3b leveling) 8.2 Discuss how technology can be integrated into lesson planning and instructional strategies to support learning objectives.8.3 Describe best practices for integrating technology into early childhood education in a way that is intentional, meaningful, and developmentally appropriate.8.4 Explore guidelines and recommendations from professional organizations (e.g., NAEYC, ISTE) on the appropriate use of technology with young children. Examine and self-reflect on teaching practices, ways to support young learners, sources of professional knowledge, and assumptions about the early childhood field with a spirit of inquiry. (1b leveling)9.2 Discuss how to adapt teaching methods to meet the diverse needs of young learners, including those with special needs or from diverse cultural backgrounds.9.3 Participate in collaborative reflection sessions with peers to discuss teaching practices, share experiences, and provide mutual support. subject: Education (EDUC)
description: PREREQUISITES: Demonstrated readiness for pre-College English  PROGRAM: Education - Elementary   LECTURE HOURS MIN: 3  DATE OF LAST REVISION: Fall 2024   A course that provides a general introduction to the field of teaching. Students will explore educational careers, teaching preparation, and professional expectations as well as requirements for teacher certification. Current trends and issues in education will be examined, including the science of teaching and learning. This course may be taught in face-to-face, blended, and Learn Anywhere formats.  OBSERVATIONAL FIELD EXPERIENCE STATEMENT: A 20-hour (minimum) in-person observational field experience is required for successful completion of this course. MAJOR COURSE LEARNING OBJECTIVES: Upon successful completion of this course the student will be expected to:  1. Complete a minimum of twenty (20) hours of supervised observational field experience in a classroom and reflect on the experience in relation to personal skills, dispositions, and future professional decisions.  2. Identify and appreciate the essential qualifications and personal demands of teaching as a profession. 2.1  Describe the various roles and responsibilities of a teacher. 2.2  Examine changing classroom dynamics and diverse student needs. 2.3  Discuss the importance of reflective practice to improve teaching and learning. 2.4  Explain the value of building and maintaining effective professional relationships. 2.5 Establish the significance of continued professional development for teachers. 2.6 Evaluate personal teaching dispositions and reflect on personal strengths. 2.7 Describe the role of self-assessment and reflection in professional growth.  3. Recognize the essential function of professional ethics, personal morals, and a strong value system in the role of the teacher, including the importance of confidentiality and liability issues pertaining to family/school relationships. 3.1  Discuss professional standards, legal obligations, and ethical responsibilities of educators. 3.2  Analyze the impact of societal changes on the role of teachers. 3.3 Examine personal beliefs and values related to the role of the teacher and the teaching profession. . 4. Reflect on personal reasons for entering the teaching profession and write an initial statement of educational philosophy. 4.1 Examine various philosophical approaches to teaching and learning. 4.2  Examine personal beliefs and values to determine a personal philosophy of teaching and learning. 4.3  Write an initial philosophy of teaching and learning.  5. Review current teacher licensure laws in the State of Indiana, including literacy certification. Compare this licensure process with requirements for teaching in a variety of locations, including opportunities to teach abroad. 5.1 Locate state laws around reading, teacher licensure, and reading difficulties. 5.2 Discuss the International Dyslexia Association (IDA) and examine its Knowledge and Practice Standards and Dispositions for Teachers of Reading. (KPS 1-5) 5.3 Compare and contrast teacher licensure in Indiana to requirements in other states and countries. 5.4 Analyze recent educational and political policies and their impact on teaching and learning. 5.5 Describe the roles, responsibilities, and required certifications associated with different teaching roles and careers in education. 5.6 Reflect on personal goals and opportunities to prepare for licensure in a desired professional role. 5.7 Explore education systems in other countries and contrast their practices with the American education system. 5.8 Compare/contrast opportunities to teach locally and abroad and examine personal choices related to future teaching opportunities.  6. Recognize and identify strategies to support the family’s role as the child’s first teacher and to support the family/teacher partnership in a culturally competent manner. 6.1  Identify personal biases and their impact on collaborating with families and creating an inclusive classroom environment. 6.2  Discuss the impact of cultural and linguistic diversity on students’ classroom experience. 6.3 Identify how environmental, cultural, and social factors contribute to literacy development. (KPS 1.5) 6.4  Associate strategies for actively including families in their children’s learning.  7. Define and describe the nature, purpose and responsibilities of the public education system in a democratic society. 7.1  Examine the reasons public education is important to maintain a democratic American society. 7.2  Discuss the differences between public and private education and their impacts on current culture. 7.3 Investigate current issues in education policy and reform.  8. Examine the history of American education and identify the philosophical foundations of education and their global roots. 8.1  Examine possible cultural and philosophical biases that are built into the American educational system. 8.2 Analyze the impact of significant educational legislation, key historical milestones and reforms over time. 8.3  Discuss the evolving nature of public education in society.  9. Discuss the Science of Teaching and Learning 9.1 Identify major research findings regarding teaching and learning. (KPS 1.6) 9.2 Define the Instructional Hierarchy. 9.3 Discuss the foundational aspects of human learning, including short and long-term memory. 10. Describe the continuum of appropriate teaching methods for children and adolescents, from discovery to explicit instruction. 10.1 Define explicit instruction and other instructional methods. 10.2 Discuss the importance of explicit instruction for teaching reading and other academic skills. (KPS 1.2) 10.3. Discuss considerations for using multisensory and multimodal language-learning techniques to enhance student engagement and memory. (KPS 4A.2) 10.4 Choose the appropriate level of support for students’ learning. 10.5 Explore the general principles and practices of structured language and literacy teaching, including explicit, systematic, cumulative, teacher-directed instruction. (KPS 4A.1) 10.6 Identify different methods of assessment and how to effectively evaluate student learning.  11. Observe and evaluate, in the classroom, various elements of diversity that affect K-12 student learning and accomplishment. 11.1 Observe and examine the many types of diversity represented in a local classroom. 11.2 Explain how social factors such as class, race, and gender affect educational outcomes. 11.3 Explore statistical evidence of diversity across different states. 11.4  Define cultural competence and its importance in educational settings. 11.5  Discuss the role of education in promoting equity among diverse populations. 11.6  Explore and reflect on implicit biases and their impact on teaching and learning. 11.7  Discuss the sources of wide differences in students’ vocabularies. (KPS 4E.2) 11.8 Observe and evaluate a classroom for its multicultural and inclusive environment, materials and practices. 12. Select one or more relevant Education Portfolio artifacts to demonstrate competency in one of the ten InTASC (Interstate Teacher Assessment and Support Consortium) Standards/CEC (Council for Exceptional Children) Standards, as applicable. description: PREREQUISITES: Demonstrated readiness for College English  PROGRAM: Education - Elementary   LECTURE HOURS MIN: 3  DATE OF LAST REVISION: Fall 2024   Examines the physical, social, emotional, cognitive, linguistic, and moral development of the child from birth through adolescence with a focus on the K-12 school-aged child. Basic theories of child development, biological and environmental foundations of development, and the study of children through observation and interviewing techniques are explored. The influence of families, peers, the school environment, culture, and the media are discussed.  OBSERVATIONAL FIELD EXPERIENCE STATEMENT:Observational Field Experience in an educational environment may be required as part of this course. MAJOR COURSE LEARNING OBJECTIVES: Upon successful completion of this course the student will be expected to: 1. Explore the physical, social, emotional, cognitive, linguistic, and moral development of the child from birth through adolescence. 1.1  Identify the role of genetics and environmental factors in child development. 1.2  Outline the developmental stages from prenatal to the newborn baby. 1.3  Identify typical growth patterns of the body and brain. 1.4 Locate threats to the health and well-being of children and ways to prevent them. 1.5  Recall how all areas of development are interrelated by applying knowledge of the various domains of development. 1.6 Discuss phases in the typical developmental progression of oral language, phoneme awareness, decoding skills, printed word recognition, spelling, reading fluency, reading comprehension, and written expression. (KPS 1.8) 2. Investigate the role of the brain in learning and literacy development. 2.1 Identify aspects of cognition and behavior that affect reading and writing development. (KPS 1.4) 2.2 Identify major research findings regarding the contribution of linguistic and cognitive factors to the prediction of literacy outcomes. (The Big 5, Simple View) (KPS 1.6) 2.3 Discuss that reading is not a natural process. Children are not born readers. 2.4 Explain that learning to read, for most people, requires explicit instruction. (KPS 1.2) 2.5 Discuss that literacy is based in language; emphasize the importance of oral language (talking, narrating experiences). 2.6 Discuss the sources of wide differences in students’ vocabularies. 2.7 Discuss historical and current practices in the teaching of reading. 3. Analyze theories of growth and development that focus on early and middle childhood through the adolescent years. 3.1  Distinguish between Piaget, Vygotsky, Erikson, Kolberg, and Bronfenbreener’s theories and the role they play in development from infancy to adolescence. 3.2  Compare and contrast each theorist’s views of development. 3.3  Connect knowledge of various theories of growth and development to real-world situations. 4. Examine and implement observation and interviewing skills as a means of understanding the child and multiple influences on the child’s development. 4.1 Identify how environmental, cultural, and social factors contribute to literacy development. (KPS 1.5) 4.2 Interpret observational data to identify patterns and significant influences on the child’s development. 4.3 Synthesize information gathered from observations and interviews to create a well-rounded profile of the child’s development. 5. Discuss the purposes for screening, progress-monitoring, diagnostic, and outcome assessments in all areas of a child’s development, including literacy development. 5.1 Describe the differences among and purposes for screening, progress-monitoring, diagnostic, and outcome assessments. (KPS 3.1) 5.2 Differentiate the relevance and importance of these assessments in identifying developmental milestones, strengths, and areas needing support. 6. Discuss confidentiality when working with children/adolescents and families. 6.1 Define confidentiality when working with children/adolescents and families. 6.2  Determine in which circumstances confidentiality should be practiced. 6.3  Compare laws and regulations related to confidentiality in educational settings, such as FERPA, and professional ethical guidelines. 7. Identify environments that promote healthy social/emotional development for all children/adolescents. 7.1  Explain appropriate environments that promote healthy emotional/social development in prenatal development, at birth, and with the newborn. 7.2  Explain appropriate environments that promote healthy emotional/social development in infancy through adolescence. 8. Recognize appropriate personal strengths and behaviors (dispositions) for adults working with school-aged children. 8.1  Identify personal strengths and areas of improvement as it relates to working with school-age children and adolescents through self-reflection. 8.2  Define professional dispositions critical for educators, including a commitment to equity, ethical behavior, and a positive attitude towards diversity. 8.3 Determine how these dispositions influence classroom management, student engagement, and the overall learning experience. 9. Identify and analyze societal issues facing today’s children/adolescents. 9.1  Research key societal issues affecting children and adolescents today, such as mental health challenges, bullying, substance abuse, and digital media influences. 9.2 Assess how societal issues influence the physical, emotional, social, and cognitive development of children and adolescents. 9.3  Devise ways to educate parents and teachers about key societal issues facing today’s children and adolescents. 10. Examine how environmental, cultural, and social factors contribute to growth and development including literacy in the culturally responsive classroom. 10.1 Identify the impact of various factors; such as but not limited to, religious background, sexual orientation, gender identity, culture, family unit, and economic status on the personal growth and development of children and adolescents. 10.2 Define implicit biases and cultural competence. 10.3 Examine the ways implicit bias can impact a teacher’s perceptions of children and families. 10.4 Determine ways to use students’ oral heritage language to facilitate English literacy development. 10.5 Recognize a framework for adapting instruction to accommodate individual differences in cognitive, linguistic, sociocultural, and behavioral aspects of learning. 11. Identify community and school resources needed to support children and families from birth through adolescence. 11.1  Research and list local community resources that provide support services for children and families, such as healthcare clinics, mental health services, recreational programs, nutrition, housing assistance, financial support, and social services. 11.2  Review programs that promote family engagement and parent education, such as family nights, workshops, and parent-teacher organizations. 11.3 Locate the availability and effectiveness of school-based resources, including counseling services, special education programs, extracurricular activities, and after-school care. 12. Select one or more relevant Education Portfolio artifacts to demonstrate competency in one of the ten InTASC (Interstate Teacher Assessment and Support Consortium) Standards/CEC (Council for Exceptional Children) Standards, as applicable. CEC ​​Initial Special Education Preparation Standards Initial Preparation Standard 1:  Learner Development and Individual Learning Differences 1.0 Beginning special education professionals understand how exceptionalities may interact with development and learning and use this knowledge to provide meaningful and challenging learning experiences for individuals with exceptionalities. Key Elements 1.1 Beginning special education professionals understand how language, culture, and family background influence the learning of individuals with exceptionalities. 1.2 Beginning special education professionals use understanding of development and individual differences to respond to the needs of individuals with exceptionalities. Initial Preparation Standard 2: Learning Environments 2.0 Beginning special education professionals create safe, inclusive, culturally responsive learning environments so that individuals with exceptionalities become active and effective learners and develop emotional well being, positive social interactions, and self-determination. Key Elements 2.1 Beginning special education professionals, through collaboration with general educators and other colleagues, create safe, inclusive, culturally responsive learning environments to engage individuals with exceptionalities in meaningful learning activities and social interactions. 2.2 Beginning special education professionals use motivational and instructional interventions to teach individuals with exceptionalities how to adapt to different environments. 2.3 Beginning special education professionals know how to intervene safely and appropriately with individuals with exceptionalities in crisis. Initial Preparation Standard 3: Curricular Content Knowledge 3.0 Beginning special education professionals use knowledge of general and specialized curricula to individualize learning for individuals with exceptionalities. Key Elements 3.1 Beginning special education professionals understand the central concepts, structures of the discipline, and tools of inquiry of the content areas they teach, and can organize this knowledge, integrate cross-disciplinary skills, and develop meaningful learning progressions for individuals with exceptionalities. 3.2 Beginning special education professionals understand and use general and specialized content knowledge for teaching across curricular content areas to individualize learning for individuals with exceptionalities. 3.3 Beginning special education professionals modify general and specialized curricula to make them accessible to individuals with exceptionalities. Initial Preparation Standard 4: Assessment 4.0 Beginning special education professionals use multiple methods of assessment and data sources in making educational decisions. Key Elements 4.1 Beginning special education professionals select and use technically sound formal and informal assessments that minimize bias. 4.2 Beginning special education professionals use knowledge of measurement principles and practices to interpret assessment results and guide educational decisions for individuals with exceptionalities. 4.3 Beginning special education professionals, in collaboration with colleagues and families, use multiple types of assessment information in making decisions about individuals with exceptionalities. 4.4 Beginning special education professionals engage individuals with exceptionalities to work toward quality learning and performance and provide feedback to guide them. Initial Preparation Standard 5: Instructional Planning and Strategies 5.0 Beginning special education professionals select, adapt, and use a repertoire of evidence-based instructional strategies to advance learning of individuals with exceptionalities. Key Elements 5.1 Beginning special education professionals consider individual abilities, interests, learning environments, and cultural and linguistic factors in the selection, development, and adaptation of learning experiences for individuals with exceptionalities. 5.2 Beginning special education professionals use technologies to support instructional assessment, planning, and delivery for individuals with exceptionalities. 5.3 Beginning special education professionals are familiar with augmentative and alternative communication systems and a variety of assistive technologies to support the communication and learning of individuals with exceptionalities. 5.4 Beginning special education professionals use strategies to enhance language development and communication skills of individuals with exceptionalities. 5.5 Beginning special education professionals develop and implement a variety of education and transition plans for individuals with exceptionalities across a wide range of settings and different learning experiences in collaboration with individuals, families, and teams. 5.6 Beginning special education professionals teach to mastery and promote generalization of learning. 5.7 Beginning special education professionals teach cross-disciplinary knowledge and skills such as critical thinking and problem solving to individuals with exceptionalities. Initial Preparation Standard 6: Professional Learning and Ethical Practice 6.0 Beginning special education professionals use foundational knowledge of the field and their professional ethical principles and practice standards to inform special education practice, to engage in lifelong learning, and to advance the profession. Key Elements 6.1 Beginning special education professionals use professional ethical principles and professional practice standards to guide their practice. 6.2 Beginning special education professionals understand how foundational knowledge and current issues influence professional practice. 6.3 Beginning special education professionals understand that diversity is a part of families, cultures, and schools, and that complex human issues can interact with the delivery of special education services. 6.4 Beginning special education professionals understand the significance of lifelong learning and participate in professional activities and learning communities. 6.5 Beginning special education professionals advance the profession by engaging in activities such as advocacy and mentoring. 6.6 Beginning special education professionals provide guidance and direction to paraeducators, tutors, and volunteers. Initial Preparation Standard 7: Collaboration 7.0 Beginning special education professionals collaborate with families, other educators, related service providers, individuals with exceptionalities, and personnel from community agencies in culturally responsive ways to address the needs of individuals with exceptionalities across a range of learning experiences. Key Elements 7.1 Beginning special education professionals use the theory and elements of effective collaboration. 7.2 Beginning special education professionals serve as a collaborative resource to colleagues. 7.3 Beginning special education professionals use collaboration to promote the well being of individuals with exceptionalities across a wide range of settings and collaborators. CEC ​​Initial Special Education Preparation Standards Initial Preparation Standard 1:  Learner Development and Individual Learning Differences 1.0 Beginning special education professionals understand how exceptionalities may interact with development and learning and use this knowledge to provide meaningful and challenging learning experiences for individuals with exceptionalities. Key Elements 1.1 Beginning special education professionals understand how language, culture, and family background influence the learning of individuals with exceptionalities. 1.2 Beginning special education professionals use understanding of development and individual differences to respond to the needs of individuals with exceptionalities. Initial Preparation Standard 2: Learning Environments 2.0 Beginning special education professionals create safe, inclusive, culturally responsive learning environments so that individuals with exceptionalities become active and effective learners and develop emotional well being, positive social interactions, and self-determination. Key Elements 2.1 Beginning special education professionals, through collaboration with general educators and other colleagues, create safe, inclusive, culturally responsive learning environments to engage individuals with exceptionalities in meaningful learning activities and social interactions. 2.2 Beginning special education professionals use motivational and instructional interventions to teach individuals with exceptionalities how to adapt to different environments. 2.3 Beginning special education professionals know how to intervene safely and appropriately with individuals with exceptionalities in crisis. Initial Preparation Standard 3: Curricular Content Knowledge 3.0 Beginning special education professionals use knowledge of general and specialized curricula to individualize learning for individuals with exceptionalities. Initial Preparation Standard 5: Instructional Planning and Strategies 5.0 Beginning special education professionals select, adapt, and use a repertoire of evidence-based instructional strategies to advance learning of individuals with exceptionalities. Includes theories and practices for promoting optimal developmental growth for all learners. Develops inclusive teaching techniques. Explores public policy, inclusion, early intervention, and laws related to special education. Explores categories of special needs, including dyslexia and other reading difficulties, and provides opportunities to explore school-based services for children with exceptional needs. This course may be taught in face-to-face, blended, virtual, and Learn Anywhere formats. Identify and define the categories of disabilities and eligibility criteria as stipulated in federal (IDEA) and State (Article 7) legislation. 2.1 Know fundamental provisions of federal and state laws that pertain to learning disabilities, including dyslexia and other reading and language disability subtypes. (KPS 2.2) Explain the term LRE (Least Restrictive Environment) and how this influences the services provided to school-age children with exceptional needs. (KPS 3.1, 3.6) 5.4 Discuss interventions for struggling readers at the end of 1st grade and how intentional experiences in PreK can prevent reading difficulties. Key Elements 1.1 Beginning special education professionals understand how language, culture, and family background influence the learning of individuals with exceptionalities. 1.2 Beginning special education professionals use understanding of development and individual differences to respond to the needs of individuals with exceptionalities. Initial Preparation Standard 2: Learning Environments 2.0 Beginning special education professionals create safe, inclusive, culturally responsive learning environments so that individuals with exceptionalities become active and effective learners and develop emotional well being, positive social interactions, and self-determination. Key Elements 2.1 Beginning special education professionals, through collaboration with general educators and other colleagues, create safe, inclusive, culturally responsive learning environments to engage individuals with exceptionalities in meaningful learning activities and social interactions. 2.2 Beginning special education professionals use motivational and instructional interventions to teach individuals with exceptionalities how to adapt to different environments. 2.3 Beginning special education professionals know how to intervene safely and appropriately with individuals with exceptionalities in crisis. Initial Preparation Standard 3: Curricular Content Knowledge 3.0 Beginning special education professionals use knowledge of general and specialized curricula to individualize learning for individuals with exceptionalities. Key Elements 3.1 Beginning special education professionals understand the central concepts, structures of the discipline, and tools of inquiry of the content areas they teach, and can organize this knowledge, integrate cross-disciplinary skills, and develop meaningful learning progressions for individuals with exceptionalities. 3.2 Beginning special education professionals understand and use general and specialized content knowledge for teaching across curricular content areas to individualize learning for individuals with exceptionalities. 3.3 Beginning special education professionals modify general and specialized curricula to make them accessible to individuals with exceptionalities. Initial Preparation Standard 4: Assessment 4.0 Beginning special education professionals use multiple methods of assessment and data sources in making educational decisions. Key Elements 4.1 Beginning special education professionals select and use technically sound formal and informal assessments that minimize bias. 4.2 Beginning special education professionals use knowledge of measurement principles and practices to interpret assessment results and guide educational decisions for individuals with exceptionalities. 4.3 Beginning special education professionals, in collaboration with colleagues and families, use multiple types of assessment information in making decisions about individuals with exceptionalities. 4.4 Beginning special education professionals engage individuals with exceptionalities to work toward quality learning and performance and provide feedback to guide them. Initial Preparation Standard 5: Instructional Planning and Strategies 5.0 Beginning special education professionals select, adapt, and use a repertoire of evidence-based instructional strategies to advance learning of individuals with exceptionalities. Key Elements 5.1 Beginning special education professionals consider individual abilities, interests, learning environments, and cultural and linguistic factors in the selection, development, and adaptation of learning experiences for individuals with exceptionalities. 5.2 Beginning special education professionals use technologies to support instructional assessment, planning, and delivery for individuals with exceptionalities. 5.3 Beginning special education professionals are familiar with augmentative and alternative communication systems and a variety of assistive technologies to support the communication and learning of individuals with exceptionalities. 5.4 Beginning special education professionals use strategies to enhance language development and communication skills of individuals with exceptionalities. 5.5 Beginning special education professionals develop and implement a variety of education and transition plans for individuals with exceptionalities across a wide range of settings and different learning experiences in collaboration with individuals, families, and teams. 5.6 Beginning special education professionals teach to mastery and promote generalization of learning. 5.7 Beginning special education professionals teach cross-disciplinary knowledge and skills such as critical thinking and problem solving to individuals with exceptionalities. Initial Preparation Standard 6: Professional Learning and Ethical Practice 6.0 Beginning special education professionals use foundational knowledge of the field and their professional ethical principles and practice standards to inform special education practice, to engage in lifelong learning, and to advance the profession. Key Elements 6.1 Beginning special education professionals use professional ethical principles and professional practice standards to guide their practice. 6.2 Beginning special education professionals understand how foundational knowledge and current issues influence professional practice. 6.3 Beginning special education professionals understand that diversity is a part of families, cultures, and schools, and that complex human issues can interact with the delivery of special education services. 6.4 Beginning special education professionals understand the significance of lifelong learning and participate in professional activities and learning communities. 6.5 Beginning special education professionals advance the profession by engaging in activities such as advocacy and mentoring. 6.6 Beginning special education professionals provide guidance and direction to paraeducators, tutors, and volunteers. Initial Preparation Standard 7: Collaboration 7.0 Beginning special education professionals collaborate with families, other educators, related service providers, individuals with exceptionalities, and personnel from community agencies in culturally responsive ways to address the needs of individuals with exceptionalities across a range of learning experiences. Key Elements 7.1 Beginning special education professionals use the theory and elements of effective collaboration. 7.2 Beginning special education professionals serve as a collaborative resource to colleagues. 7.3 Beginning special education professionals use collaboration to promote the well being of individuals with exceptionalities across a wide range of settings and collaborators.
